extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of literature, drama, and creative writers studying Aristotle's Poetics
extracted.subtask_description: Guiding principles and evaluative criteria for poetry, music, dance and drama drawn from Aristotle's Poetics and scholarly commentary — covering what counts as imitation, the components of verse and music, character-portrayal, form (narrative vs dramatic), and aesthetic effects. Useful for analysing or producing classical-style verse/drama and for understanding mimesis-based critique.

rubrics_metrics.name: Harmony (tune, not chords)
rubrics_metrics.description: Harmony: the author in the Problems explains that he means not chords, but tunes; the word properly means a combination of contraries (treble and bass), in this case treble and bass, simultaneously or in order.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat harmony as melodic/tuneful element rather than harmonic-chordal structure. Commentary notes debates (Watasek, Hanslick) about whether notes imitate emotions; keep harmony's role as combination of contrasting lines (treble/bass) in mind when evaluating musical or lyric components.

rubrics_metrics.name: Components of verse vs music
rubrics_metrics.description: Separate or mixed: language + rhythm give verse; harmony + the dance give music.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When analysing or composing, identify which elements (language, rhythm, harmony, dance) are operative. Verse is fundamentally language shaped by rhythm; music (in Aristotle's account) is the fusion of harmony and dance. Consider whether components occur simultaneously (some forms) or in different parts of a performance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reproductive art vs creative art
rubrics_metrics.description: Reproductive art gives some suggestions (symbols only) and produces an actual likeness of lines and colours; creative art reproduces psychic motion — music reproduces psychic motion as sound-as-motion, not merely the rhythm and harmony applied to sound.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish between works that reproduce perceptible details (reproductive) and those that evoke internal states or psychic motion (creative). Use the 'orange vs painted ball' example: reproductive art calls up associated impressions; creative art (e.g., music) should reproduce inner motion or feeling. Consider which mode the work is operating in when judging fidelity or aesthetic success.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dance as rhythm-based imitation
rubrics_metrics.description: Dancers’ measures simulate with the rhythm itself, without Harmony; for Dancers, the beating of time is necessary — dance measures portray not only moral qualities, but emotions and experiences also.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate dance primarily on rhythmic imitation and coordinated movement rather than harmonic content. Look for how footed/figured measures express moral qualities, activities (hunting, war, labour), and emotions. Consider whether dance functions as symbolic suggestion or as direct imitation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Music as imitation of forms of motion/emotion
rubrics_metrics.description: Some modern psychologists (e.g., Witasek) hold that notes actually imitate the form which the emotions take (e.g., anger as irregular swelling/sinking), while others (Hanslick) argue musical themes are sui generis; empirical test cited (audience new to a piece becoming sad/merry in accordance with the music).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing music or melodic elements in poetry/drama, consider whether the music convincingly embodies or corresponds to emotional/physical motions. Use concrete correspondences (slow movement = funeral tread, airs = tramp of armies) as a test of effective musical imitation, but be aware of counterarguments that music's affect may be intrinsic rather than representational.

rubrics_metrics.name: Portrayal of character (moral gradation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Those who portray persons must be relatively good or bad, since thus only can character regularly be classified; difference between any characters is relative badness and goodness — characters are ranged as better than, worse than, or on a level with ourselves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess character types by their moral quality (virtue/vice) and relativity to the audience's standard. Good characterisation requires that characters be placed on a moral scale (superior, average, inferior) so that distinctions are meaningful. Consider how externals and physiognomy signal these moral positions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choice of treatment: narrative vs dramatic
rubrics_metrics.description: You can present the same fiction as a narrative (past narration, possibly with role change) or as dramatic (experienced and realized by the fictitious persons in the present). The important difference is narration of the past vs realization of the present.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decide which mode (narrative or dramatic) best serves the mimesis you intend: drama requires enactment in energeia (present realization), while epic/narrative relies on report. Evaluate whether the chosen treatment suits the intended psychological immediacy and social interactions of the piece.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tragedy as imitation of realized life (actions, not mere persons)
rubrics_metrics.description: Tragedy is a fictitious realization of fully conscious life; it is not an imitation of persons but of the simulators (actors/fictitious persons) experiencing and realizing their functions — there must be more than one person, since man is a social animal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge tragedy by its portrayal of actions and causal relations enacted in the present, the social interactions and 'praxis' that give the work unity. Evaluate how well the plot's actions reveal character and produce catharsis rather than merely presenting types of persons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tune (melody) as restraining element in lyric — metre secondary
rubrics_metrics.description: In lyric poetry the language takes the form of verse (measured syllables), but the 'restraining element' is not the metre, but the tune; metre is superimposed on language and not the primary organizing principle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When composing or critiquing lyric, prioritise melodic/tuneful control (tune) over strict metrical form as the decisive shaping force. Metre may adapt to language and tune; do not conflate metre with the essence of lyric.

rubrics_metrics.name: Integration vs separation of performance components
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain forms (Dithyrambic and Nomic Poetry, Tragedy and Comedy) may employ Dance, Tune and Verse all together (simultaneously) or in different parts of the performance; the former employ them all simultaneously, the latter employ them in different parts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess genre/form by how components are combined. For works that integrate multiple arts, evaluate the coherence and balance among dance, tune, and verse; for those that separate them, consider the effectiveness of each part in its role and transitions between them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pleasure from identification and proper degree of reproduction
rubrics_metrics.description: We enjoy contemplating exact likenesses because the process is accompanied by the solution of a problem (identification of the subjects); too much reproduction reduces aesthetic pleasure — room must be left to imagination and reasoning faculties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating realism and fidelity, consider whether the work leaves enough unsaid for the audience's imagination. Effective art balances recognisable likeness with omission to provoke cognitive pleasure of identification. Technical execution (colouring, craft) may substitute if the original is unknown.

rubrics_metrics.name: Innate mimicry and use of rhythm/harmony
rubrics_metrics.description: Mimicry is innate in infants and it is natural to imitate in harmony and rhythm; children delight in harmony and rhythm, and rhythmical speech likely evolved from such instincts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exploit natural human responsiveness to rhythm and harmony in composition to increase immediacy and accessibility. Rhythm and musicality are powerful tools for engaging universal perceptual pleasures; test whether rhythmic patterns align with expected human responses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Artist's temperament determines subject/style
rubrics_metrics.description: The artist chooses the type which suits his individual temperament: the more serious will mimic fine doings (fine characters), the more frivolous will mimic ignoble doings (lampoons).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate coherence between the artist's chosen subjects/style and their temperament or voice. Authenticity and authority in depiction are enhanced when an artist's temperament aligns with the moral and tonal demands of the chosen genre.

rubrics_metrics.name: Methodological basis for classification (essentials vs accidents)
rubrics_metrics.description: A true basis of classification must be essential to the work such that it could not be withdrawn and the work still carried on; metre, for instance, would not be a true basis, because mimesis need not have metre.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When categorising genres or judging form, prioritise features that are constitutive of the work's identity (e.g., enacted action for drama) rather than accidental or variable features (e.g., metre). Use the 'withdrawal test' — if removing the feature leaves the work intact, it's not an essential basis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dance/music portray concrete subjects (hunting, war, labour)
rubrics_metrics.description: Dance measures portray experiences counterfeited by the dance: hunting, war, fishing, rowing, the life and habits of animals, and various forms of labour and domestic operations; historical evidence shows dance could make a story clear by movement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing or composing dance or movement-based sequences, consider clarity of subject-matter through gesture and rhythm. Use culturally legible motifs (e.g., marching, rowing) so that dance can function as narrative or symbolic exposition.
